title: DID REBEKAH HELP GOD’S PLAN—OR MANIPULATE IT?
paragraphs: DID REBEKAH HELP GOD’S PLAN—OR MANIPULATE IT?

She heard God’s promise before her sons were born. Years later, she lied to her husband, disguised her favorite son, and helped steal a blessing. The terrifying question is not whether God’s plan succeeded. It is whether Rebekah had forgotten that God never needed her sin to accomplish it.
There is something unsettling about Genesis 27.
Not because the Bible gives us a villain we can easily hate.
It gives us a family we can recognize.
A father with preferences.
A mother with preferences.
Two brothers competing beneath the weight of expectation.
An aging man preparing to bless the son he loves.
A mother listening from another room.
A son willing to deceive.
Another son who will soon discover that something precious has been taken from him.
And hovering above the entire house is a promise God had already spoken.
That detail changes everything.
Because Rebekah was not trying to manufacture a destiny God had never revealed.
She was trying to secure a destiny God had already promised.
And that may be one of the most dangerous spiritual places a believer can stand:
Knowing what God has said...
but becoming terrified that God will not accomplish it unless you take control.
Before Jacob and Esau were born, Rebekah experienced such violent struggling within her pregnancy that she went to inquire of the LORD.
God answered her.
The Hebrew of Genesis 25:23 contains the words:
וְרַב יַעֲבֹד צָעִיר
ve-rav ya'avod tsa'ir
Literally, in its natural contextual sense:
“The older shall serve the younger.”
The reversal was already announced.
Before Jacob could scheme.
Before Rebekah could deceive.
Before Isaac could pronounce a blessing.
Before either child had established a moral record that could explain God's choice.

Paul later reaches back to this exact moment in Romans 9. He emphasizes that the twins had not yet been born and had done neither good nor evil when God's purpose according to election was declared. In the Greek text, Romans 9:12 echoes the Genesis declaration:
Ὁ μείζων δουλεύσει τῷ ἐλάσσονι
Ho meizōn douleusei tō elassoni.
“The older will serve the younger.”
Paul's point is devastating to human pride: God's purpose did not originate in Jacob's performance.
It originated in God who calls.
Which means that before Rebekah ever formed her plan...
God already had His.
Remember that.
Because Genesis 27 becomes far more uncomfortable when you realize Rebekah was attempting to obtain through manipulation something whose ultimate outcome rested in the sovereignty of God.
Isaac had grown old.
His eyesight had failed.
He called Esau, his older son, and asked him to hunt game and prepare the food he loved. Then Isaac intended to bless him.
Rebekah was listening.
You can almost feel the tension entering the room.
Perhaps she remembered the oracle.
Perhaps the words spoken during her pregnancy had never left her.
“The older shall serve the younger.”
But now Isaac appeared ready to place the patriarchal blessing upon Esau.
What do you do when circumstances seem to be moving in the opposite direction of something God has spoken?
That is where this ancient family drama stops being ancient.
Because some of us know exactly what Rebekah's temptation feels like.
God promised...
but nothing seems to be happening.
You prayed...
but the door remained closed.
You tried to obey...
but somebody else got the opportunity.
You believed God was leading...
but circumstances began moving backward.
You thought the relationship would heal.
You thought the ministry would grow.
You thought justice would come.
You thought your child would return.
You thought the answer would have arrived by now.
And somewhere between God promised and I am still waiting, a dangerous thought enters:
Maybe I need to help God.
That thought can sound surprisingly spiritual.
You can call manipulation “wisdom.”
You can call control “discernment.”
You can call impatience “taking initiative.”
You can call dishonesty “protecting the vision.”
You can even commit something God forbids while convincing yourself that you are defending something God desires.
Rebekah moved quickly.
She told Jacob what she had heard.
Then she gave him instructions.
Bring the animals.
She would prepare the food.
Jacob would take it to his father.
Jacob immediately saw the problem.
Esau was hairy.
Jacob was smooth.
If Isaac touched him, the deception could collapse.
Jacob feared being exposed and receiving a curse instead of a blessing.
And then Rebekah said something chilling:
עָלַי קִלְלָתְךָ בְּנִי
Alai qillelatekha beni.
“Upon me be your curse, my son.”
In other words:
Let the consequences fall on me.
Just do what I say.
This is not a calm picture of faith.
This is a mother so committed to an outcome that she is willing to carry the danger of the deception herself.
She takes Esau's best garments.
She dresses Jacob in them.
She covers his hands and the smooth part of his neck with goatskins.
Then Jacob walks toward his blind father carrying food prepared by his mother.
And suddenly the story becomes almost unbearable.
Isaac hears Jacob's voice.
But he feels Esau's hands.
“The voice is Jacob's voice,” Isaac observes, “but the hands are the hands of Esau.”
Think about that sentence.
Jacob had become a man wearing someone else's identity in order to obtain something he desperately wanted.
And there are people reading this who know exactly what that feels like.
Maybe you are exhausted because you have been wearing somebody else's skin.
Pretending your marriage is fine.
Pretending your faith is strong.
Pretending you are not angry.
Pretending you are not addicted.
Pretending you have forgiven.
Pretending your ministry is healthier than it is.
Pretending you do not need help.
Pretending you are the person everybody believes you are.
Your voice says one thing.
Your hands say another.
And underneath the costume is a frightened soul wondering:
If people knew the real me, would I still be blessed?
Jacob lied.
More than once.
When Isaac asked who he was, Jacob identified himself as Esau.
When Isaac wondered how he had returned so quickly, Jacob even invoked God in explaining his success.
That is how far deception can travel.
Eventually we can begin using God's name to justify things God never told us to do.
And yet...
Jacob received the blessing.
That is where careless interpretations can become dangerous.
Someone might conclude:
“See? Rebekah was right.”
No.
A successful outcome does not automatically sanctify the method used to obtain it.
Scripture never establishes the principle that deception becomes righteous when we believe the destination is righteous.
The Bible consistently condemns falsehood and celebrates truthfulness. God's sovereignty over human sin does not transform sin into obedience.
This distinction matters enormously.
God can accomplish His purpose through the wreckage of human sin without approving the sin that created the wreckage.
Joseph's brothers sold him.
God used it to preserve life.
Their betrayal did not become righteous.
Judas betrayed Jesus.
The cross nevertheless unfolded according to God's redemptive purpose.
Judas's betrayal did not become holy.
Human evil can be incorporated into divine providence without becoming divine instruction.
That is the theological tension inside Rebekah's story.
She knew something true.
She pursued it wrongly.
And God remained sovereign anyway.
That should humble every one of us.
Because sometimes the greatest threat to obedience is not believing the wrong promise.
It is trying to fulfill the right promise the wrong way.
Rebekah's actions also produced consequences.
Esau returned.
He prepared the food.
He entered expecting his father's blessing.
And then the truth surfaced.
The blessing had already been given.
Esau's reaction is raw.
He cries out.
The family fractures.
Hatred enters the relationship between the brothers.
Esau resolves that after his father's death, he will kill Jacob.
Rebekah learns of the threat and sends Jacob away.
She expects separation.
But consider the emotional cost.
The son she loved leaves home.
Jacob heads toward Haran.
Years pass.
Genesis never records a reunion between Rebekah and Jacob.
The text does not explicitly tell us that she never saw him again, so we should not claim more than Scripture says.
But the narrative gives us no recorded reunion.
That silence hurts.
The mother who said, “Let the curse fall on me,” helped secure the immediate outcome she wanted...
and then watched her family break apart.
This is why sin is such a terrible bargain.
It often promises control over tomorrow while quietly stealing something from today.
Maybe you manipulated someone because you were afraid of losing them.
And lost their trust instead.
Maybe you lied because you were afraid of consequences.
And the lie created consequences worse than the truth.
Maybe you forced a door because you were terrified God would never open one.
Now you are standing inside something you begged for...
without peace.
Maybe nobody knows.
That may be the hardest part.
Everybody sees the blessing.
Only you remember the goatskins.
Everybody celebrates the result.
Only you know what you did to get there.
And now the enemy whispers that because your hands are dirty, God must be finished with you.
But this is where the Gospel enters the room.
Not as permission to manipulate.
Not as an excuse for sin.
Not as a sentimental way to avoid repentance.
The Gospel tells the truth about us more severely than our excuses ever will...
and offers grace more extravagantly than our shame believes possible.
Jacob's story does not end beneath goatskins.
God meets him.
God disciplines him.
God humbles him.
God wrestles with him.
God changes him.
Eventually Jacob receives another name:
Israel.
The deceiver does not remain merely “the deceiver.”
Grace begins rewriting the man.
But grace does not pretend the deception never happened.
Grace confronts.
Grace wounds pride.
Grace produces surrender.
Grace transforms.
And centuries later, from this scandal-filled covenant family comes the Messiah.
Jesus Christ.
Not because this family was morally spotless.
Because God was faithful.
That is one of the breathtaking truths running through Scripture.
The genealogy leading toward Christ is not a museum of flawless human beings.
It is filled with weakness, scandal, failure, outsiders, sinners, complicated families, and people desperately dependent upon mercy.
Then Christ comes.
And unlike Jacob, Jesus does not deceive His Father to obtain a blessing.
He perfectly obeys the Father.
Unlike Jacob, Jesus does not dress Himself as another man to steal another man's inheritance.
The eternal Son takes upon Himself our humanity and willingly goes to the cross to rescue sinners.
Jacob feared receiving a curse.
Christ willingly bore the curse for His people.
At Calvary, Jesus does not manipulate His way into blessing.
He gives Himself so that guilty people can receive blessing they could never earn.
That is why your hope is not that you can manipulate your life into becoming acceptable to God.
Your hope is Christ.
Paul's argument concerning Rebekah and her children presses precisely against boasting in human achievement: God's saving purpose rests finally in the One who calls, not in human works.
Maybe that is what you needed to hear.
God does not need your deception to preserve your destiny.
God does not need your compromise to fulfill His will.
God does not need you to become someone else before He can deal with you.
He wants truth.
Repentance.
Faith.
Surrender.
Maybe your Rebekah moment is happening right now.
You see something slipping away.
You are tempted to manipulate.
To send the message.
To twist the story.
To hide the evidence.
To control the person.
To manufacture the opportunity.
To force the relationship.
To exaggerate the testimony.
To make the numbers look better.
To compromise quietly because you have convinced yourself that the final outcome will somehow glorify God.
Don't put on the goatskins.
If God has truly called you, you do not need sin to keep His purposes alive.
Obedience may cost you the outcome you wanted today.
But disobedience can cost things you never intended to lose.
And if you already did it...
if you are already standing there wearing the evidence of decisions you regret...
come into the light.
Jesus did not die only for respectable sins.
He died for liars.
Manipulators.
Scheming people.
Controlling people.
Religious people.
Broken people.
People who knew better.
People who promised never again and failed again.
People like Jacob.
People like us.
Repentance is not telling God a secret.
He already knows.
Repentance is finally agreeing with God about the thing you have been defending.
Stop calling control wisdom.
Stop calling compromise necessity.
Stop calling deception protection.
Take off the goatskins.
Come honestly to Christ.
Confess.
Turn.
Receive mercy.
And then make right what you can.
The astonishing message of Christianity is not that good people can maintain spotless reputations.
It is that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
This is From Scandal to Grace.
Not because scandal does not matter.
Because scandal does not get the final word when a sinner comes to Christ.
Jesus does.
Because eventually most of us encounter a moment when God's timing feels unbearably slow and control begins masquerading as faith.

Supporting Gospel-centered ministry financially is not a condition of glorifying God, salvation, blessing, or spiritual maturity; the Gospel cannot be purchased. But voluntary generosity can genuinely help Gospel work reach and disciple more people.
The discount is gratitude for your support—not a promise of spiritual blessing and never a price placed on the Gospel.
Trust Christ.
Tell the truth.
Repent quickly.
Refuse to manipulate what belongs in God's hands.
And remember Rebekah the next time fear whispers that God's promise needs your sin to survive.
Because perhaps the most frightening thing about Genesis 27 is not that Rebekah stopped believing God's promise.
Perhaps she still believed it.
She simply stopped trusting God with how it would happen.
And maybe that is the question now sitting quietly in front of you:
What are you currently trying to control because somewhere deep inside, you are afraid God cannot be trusted with it?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Share it with the person whose hands are getting tired from trying to control everything.
And never forget this:
God's promises do not need the disguise of your manipulation; when your schemes collapse and your hands are finally empty, those empty hands may become the very hands that learn how to receive grace.
